title: My AI-generated game worlds keep coming out peaceful. How do you inject conflict?
author: lukinator644
selftext:
I'm building Altworld, a browser-based life sim. Players describe a world and the AI turns it into a playable scenario. You create a character and act turn by turn with natural language. The World Forge feature can take anything from 'cyberpunk Tokyo' to 'medieval Persia' and generate a setting.

The generation gives a few NPCs and a location, but after a couple turns it often feels static. There's no built-in conflict. We've been trying a second pass that reads the prompt for implied tensions. It seeds things like a drought or a rival faction if the prompt suggests frontier hardship.

It helps, but we still sometimes get peaceful stasis. What approaches have you tried to make procedural worlds feel alive from the first turn?

comments.author: orblabs
comments.body: Had vaguely similar problems some time ago, but it is hard to suggest anything knowing nothing about the structure of your game etc. one very simple system they you can probably adapt to your case is to, every x turns, pick a card of sorts with some predefined generic narrative tropes that then get fed to the LLM together with whatever else you prompt it for that turn.

comments.author: NovelFlame_AI
comments.body:
I ran into something similar a while back. A lot of generated worlds end up feeling peaceful because nobody actually wants anything badly enough.

What helped me was thinking less about events and more about competing goals. If the merchant wants one thing, the mayor wants another, and the local faction wants something else entirely, conflict tends to emerge on its own. People are usually more interesting than disasters anyway.
